hints: Focus on what the vaccine actually left behind in the body, memory cells with receptors shaped to fit the original flu antigen exactly.
Ask yourself which type of response needs that exact fit to be fast, and which type happens from scratch when the fit is lost.
walkthrough:
**Recall what vaccination gives you**

Vaccination triggers a primary response to the vaccine strain and leaves behind memory B and T cells.

Those memory cells are highly specific. Their receptors only recognise the original antigen shape.

**See what mutation does**

Mutation in the antigen gene changes the shape of the antigenic protein.

Think lock and key. The old memory cell key no longer fits the new mutated lock, so the memory cells do not recognise it and cannot launch a fast response.

**Sort primary versus secondary**

Because there is no recognition, there is no rapid secondary response to the mutated virus. That makes statement 2 true and statement 3 true.

The body must start again from naive lymphocytes, so the person WILL make a slow primary response to the new antigen. That makes statement 1 false. So only 2 and 3 are correct.

options.A: Includes statement 1, which is wrong because the person will still make a slow primary response to the new, unrecognised antigen.
options.B: Wrong on both sides, statement 1 is false and it leaves out the true statement 3 about memory cells failing to recognise the mutant.
options.C: Includes true statement 3 but also false statement 1, and misses true statement 2 about loss of the secondary response.
options.D: Correct, memory cells do not recognise the changed antigen (3), so no fast secondary response occurs (2), only a slow primary response.
